author: La Tour Landry, Geoffroy de, 14th cent.
title: [Here begynneth the booke which the knyght of the toure made,
text:
in due time / as about the hour of tyerce / at mid day / at souper at hour covenable / after the time / For such life as you have used & maintained in your youth. you would maintain



and use in your old age

aLso my dear Daughters / you aught to fast till that be married three or four days in the week. For  to adaunt your flesh / that it mue not  / for to keep you more clean and holily in  of God / Whiche shall keep and guerdome you double / And if you may not fast the three days / yet at the lest  in thonoure of the precious blood and of the passion of Ihesu  that suffered death for us / And if you fast it not to breed &  at lest take no thing that suffers death / For it is a Much  thing as I have heard tell of a knight a Much noble man  was in a battle of Crysten men against the sarasyne / It  that a Crysten man had his heed smyten of with a  and spack after till that the Priest cam / and confessed him / And he demanded of him / for what merit it was that he  speak without the body. And the heed answered him / that no  ode deed was done to God / but that it gate grace. And that he  kept the Wednesday from eating of flesh in thonoure of the  of God· that was Then sold / And the Friday he eat no  that suffered death / And for this service God would not that he should be dampened / ne that he should day in deadly sin / whereof he was not confessed / This is a Much fair example / and aught to be re¦membryd / that such thing as suffers death aught not be eaten on the Friday / And also my fair Daughters / it is Much good to has¦te the Saturday / in thonoure of our lady and of her holy vyrgy¦nyte / to th'end that she get grace for you for to keep clean your virginity and your chastity in the grace of God. and in the lo¦ue of your friends / that none evil temptations over mastery you not / And hit is a great victory against the flesh / and a Much holy thing / And I say to you for truth / that it shall be to you a light thing / if you acustomme you therein / For it is but acustomaunce for to here the mass / and the service of God / for to say your hours. and to do all other holy works / as ha¦ue done these holy Women / like as it is contained in the legēdis



And in the lives of the saints of heaven

tHenne I would that you knew example of a foolish woman that fasted the Friday / of whom I shall tell to you the history / Ther was a foolish woman in the Cy¦te of Rome / that alway fasted the Friday in thonoure of the pas¦syon of sweet Ihesu Criste· And the Saturday in thonoure of the Vyrgynyte of our lady / And alway these two days she kept surely· Hit happened on a night that she went to ward her love / whn it was dark / And suddenly or she was beware / she fell in to a pit· which was twenty fathom deep / And as she was falling / she escried with and hyhe voice / lady help / and she fill upon the water / and found it hard as a plank.

author: Virgil. Aeneis.
title: Here fynyssheth the boke yf [sic] Eneydos, compyled by Vyrgyle, which hathe be translated oute of latyne in to frenshe, and oute of frenshe reduced in to Englysshe by me wyll[ia]m Caxton, the xxij. daye of Iuyn. the yere of our lorde. M.iiij.Clxxxx. The fythe yere of the regne of kynge Henry the seuenth
text: And went and determined herself for to fulfil the commaundemnt of her said sister Elysse. and to do all by order that that she had charged her for to do/ The which things thus done of the queen dydo/ willing to proceed to her said sacrifice. went to see the place where the great fire should be. kendled which she found all ready made garnissed with agrete quantity of logs and under h●m and round about great foison of dry faggots & other small wood for to kindle the fire lightly/ & took herself for to incense it and to susfounge the place/ And crowned it with garlands made of herbs and branches that men have of costume to put upon the corces of the deed bodies upon their graves and tombs and also over the image and figure of aeneas that she had do make after the semblaunce of him for to be brent there with her. And took the sword that he had left with her that she hidded in the same place for to accomplish the work that she thought for to do/ after she weld go with the said prestresse to her sacrifice of magic that she had ordained to be do/ and were the temples and awtiers well prepared and garnished of oblations and other things necessayre and convenable to this present obsequy And then came out the old witch of charmouse magyque in her raiments made in diverse manners all her head shaven for to fuldoo her sacrifices/ Atte the beginning of which she invoqued and called three times by hideous words three hundred gods infernal/ and the great habitation of hell sempyternalle who their confusion/ the mother of magyque in her triple proportion. and the three faces of the moan that shineth by the quarfours sometime with two great horns and sometime as it were cut by the mids/ Another time she appyereth all round. whereof many one been marvelled/ By cause that they ygnore the causes/ the which if they knew them they should not happily marvel. Also from within it is obscured moche more in some places than in some other. So that men might say that it encloseth that it is the triple figure of the verge dyane. whereof maketh her Invocation this lady old magicienne/ And thus doing she dide asperse the place with the waters obscure venomous and black representing the liquor of the hideous fountains of hell/ After she maketh to be brought to her certain herbs fresh and new mown & taken by night when the moan shineth with sercles of copper whereof the juice is passing venymouse and of colour all black And with this she taketh the little skin that remaineth of the secondyne within the forehead of the little fool that must be scraped away from his forehead when he is newly borne afore that the mother licketh it of/ whereof after that done he shall not be known of his said mother/ as it is said.

author: Virgil. Aeneis.
title: Here fynyssheth the boke yf [sic] Eneydos, compyled by Vyrgyle, which hathe be translated oute of latyne in to frenshe, and oute of frenshe reduced in to Englysshe by me wyll[ia]m Caxton, the xxij. daye of Iuyn. the yere of our lorde. M.iiij.Clxxxx. The fythe yere of the regne of kynge Henry the seuenth
text: that thou take the vestiments & the mitre upon thy heed for to fulmake th oblation to pluto the great god of hell admiral of the styge/ which is a great pound of fire brenninge that runneth through all hell/ composed & made of brimstone & of pitch/ this immolation I have purposed to do unto him with my busy thought for to put an end my great tribul●coˉns & care ennuyouse/ for the which cause I will kindle a great fire for to brenn the raiments of aeneas his image that are left with me/ wherewith I shall do sacrifice to ● great flood infernal. to th end he be moved with hate against him/ when by death his trist soul shall be delivered to him after these things. this said barthe went her way hastily as her old age might suffer it. & left there her master's dido the quyvered & shook of great rage & enured into a great fransie desiring taccomplysshe the purpose of her death/ whereof the dreadful remembrance ready to be executed. troubled her in such wise. that it made all her wits to torn in to a wicked kind and in a mind for to destroy the first composition coagulate in covenable proportion for the entreteynyge of the spirit vital. whereof her fair eyen grieve and laughing were incontinent turned in to a right hidouse looking mobile & sangwynouse to see/ the sweet ball of the eye which is the very receptacle interyor of light visible/ and judge of the colours by reflection obgectyf which she bringeth unto the Impression cogytyve of the intendment/ whereof she maketh a present to the suppost indicatyf discerning without interualle the differences abstractyve adhering to their subject. was soon made obscure & her light impeached from the very judging in perfect knowledge/ her tender chykes and visage that afore was pleasant & debonnayre of sangwyne colour to urning upon white/ became all pale suddenly in hydouse manner & all mortified for the cruel death whereof the hard angwysshes had enuahyshed her already. & with great fury betaken & cast went & mounted the degrees sll high upon her palace till that she came there as the wood was assembled for to kindle there a fire. In which place the habilements the bed & the other things with the Image of aeneas & also his sword. were brought for to be brent & cast out of memory the which dydo all thus vexed & troubled in her wits drew the sword out of the shethe for to murder & slay herself. b●t or ever she would do this. she dide look upon the habilimentes/ the bed & other remnant. that by other times afore had plaised her so moche/ & thenne she began somewhat for to lacryme & sigh upon the bed where she put herself inproferring her last words in this manner: O right sweet dispoillynges plaisaunt well loved & honoured of me sometime aslonge as god & fortune would.

author: Pierre, de la Cépède, 15th cent.
title: Thystorye of the right noble and worthy knyght parys and of the fayre vyenne the dolphyns doughter of vyennoys.
text:

vaynqynysshed loyally ād well For

author: Joannes, of Hildesheim, d. 1375.
title: [The lyfe of the thre kynges of Coleyne]
text:
and tornyth with the wind as a fane/ And through the light of the son by day & of the moan by night the same star giveth light a great way in to the country about/ And many other marvels been told of this hill of Vaws/

When the time of mercy & grace was come that god would have mercy on mankind/ when the father of heaven sent down his son to take flesh & blood of our lady saint Mary & to be borne of her for our salvation/ In that time the Emperor of Rome Octavian held the empire of all the world/ In the year of his empire xlij as saint Luke telleth he sent out a commandment to describe all the world( Exiit edictum & c̈) And the discriving was first under Cirinus that was bishop of Syrie/ And every man went home to his own country/ then go joseph out of Galilee in to Nazareth in the Jewry. and that was king David's land. the which city was called Bethlehem. By cause joseph was of the house & of the main of king David. therefore he go in to his country with his wife our lady saint Mary great with child/ So when they were there. the time was come that our lady should be delivered/ And so she was delivered by goddies own might & ministration of angels. she wrapped him in clothes & laid him in a manger. for there was none other place ¶ And ye shall understand that Bethlehem was never of great reputation nor place of great quantity. but it hath a good fundament/ For there been many caves under the earth/ And Bethlehem is fro Iherusalem but two miles/ It is but a castle. but it is called a city by cause king David was borne there/ And in that town was sometime an house of isaiah that was father to king David. in the which house king David was borne & anointed to be king of Israel by Samuel the prophet/ And in the same place christ was born God's son of heaven/ And that place was sometime in the end of a street that was called the covered street/ And this was the cause why it was so called. for the great heat & brenning of the son it was so covered with black clothes & other clothes to keep away the heat of the son. and so it is yet to this day/ And in that street was wont to be a market once in the week of old clothes and other things. and specially of timber/ In that strete stood sometime an house. and isaiah king David's father left a little house before a den under the either. and it was shapen like a little cellar/ isaiah the father of David and other after them put in that cave certain necessaries that longed to household for heat of the son/ It is also the manere in all the country both in cytces and towns to be certain houses that been called there Alchan.

author: Joannes, of Hildesheim, d. 1375.
title: [The lyfe of the thre kynges of Coleyne]
text: that in the same day when god was borne. were seen many sons. but when the day of christmas was passed. the star ascended up in to the firmament/ And the star that thus was showed was no thing like the stars that been painted here in diverse places/ For it had right many streaks and beemies more bright brenning than a brand of fire/ And as an Eagle fleeing & beating the air with his wings. right so the streaks & the beemes of that moved themself about/ And the star had in himself the form & the likeness of a young child. and above him the sign of a Cross/ And a voice was herd in the star saying) Natus est nobis hody rex judeorum qui est expectacō gencium & dominator eorum ite ad inquirendum eum & adorandum) that is to say/ This day is borne to us king of the jews that folk have abiden and he is lord of them god forth and seek him and do him worshypp/ Therefore for strengthing of our faith & to affirm this matter foresaid almighty god whose providence in his ordinance fayllyth not/ ¶ And saint Paul saith) Vocatea que non sunt tanquam ea que sunt) that is to say/ God calleth those that been not aswell as those that been of his providence/ Thus he died and disposed. as he died in the old Testament. when he gave a language to an ass. and made an ass to speak to Balaam/ He would in the begynnning of the new Testament give a voice to speak out of a sterie that the same Balaam prophesied of/ ¶ When all the people of that country abowtesawe this wonderful and marvelous star. and also heard the voice of the star. they were greatly afraid. and had great wonder thereof/ But they knew well that it was the same star that was prophesied of by Balaam. and long time was desired and abiden of all the people of that country theraboute. Thus when these three Kings that the time reigned in Ynde. Chaldee and perfidy weren informed and well assured by the Astronomers and by the prophecies of this star/ They were right glad that they had grace to see that star in their days that was long time prophesied afore. and all the people had so long looked after/ Wherefore though each of these three kings weren far from other. and none of them knew of others purpose. yet in one hour the star appeared to them all three/ And then they ordained and purposed them anon with great and rich gifts and many diverse ornaments that were belonging unto the degree & array of kings. and also with mules & camels and horses charged with precious treasures & with great number and multitude of people to go seek in their best array and to worship our lord Ihesu christ that was borne to be Saviour of all the world and the king of jews that was born that tyme.

author: Joannes, of Hildesheim, d. 1375.
title: [The lyfe of the thre kynges of Coleyne]
text:
that same angel it was whose voice was herd in the star. and that go so forth with the star before the three kings/ For when the three kings spoke with the shepherds. the star more & more began to shine brighter & brighter ¶ these three kings were the first of miscreants that believed on christ. and the shepherds were the first of jews that believed on christ/ And all though the kings were no jewewes yet they said that they came to worship the king of jews/

When the kings had spoken with the sheep herds. then they gave them great gifts and so road forth to Bethlehem/ then anon as they were come unto Bethlehem they lighted down of their horses & changed their array. and clothed them in the best and richest clothes that they had/ And as kings should be arrayed they arrayed themself/ And always the star go forth tofore them/ And the nearer that they came to the place the more the star shined brighter and brighter/ And then they road thorough the covered street as it is told afore till they came to the little house where in Crste was borne/ And the star stood still upon the ground tofore the door/ And anon after the star departed himself in so great light. that the little house & the cave within was full of light/ And so anon the star ascended up in to the air. and there stood still alway in the same place. as it is said in the gospel tofore( Et intrantes domum & c̈) And entering in to the house they found our lady & her child. and fell down and worshipped him and offered to him gifts. Gold. Myrrh. and incense/ ¶ Of this came afterward an use in that country of the east/ There shall no man come in the presence of the Sultan. or of a king to speak with him but he have gold or silver or some other richesse in his hands/ And also or he speak with the Sultan he shall kiss the ground/ And this is used in that country unto this day/ ¶ furthermore frere Minours when they shall come to the Sultan or to a king they must offer to him peers or apples/ For they may touch no gold nor silver/ And the Sultan receiveth the peers or apples with reverence & meekness/ ¶ And that time that these three kings offeed thus to christ. he was in his manhood. a little child of xiij days of age/ And he lay wraped in clothes of little value in his mothers lap/ ¶ As it is written in diverse books she was in person fleshly. and somewhat brown/ And in presence of these three kings she was covered with a poor white mantel. and that she held close tofore her with her lift hand/ And her heed was covered all together save her face with a linen cloth/ And she sat upon the maynger/ And with her right hand she held up god almighty's heed/ So after these three kings had worshipped god & kissed his hands right devoutly.

author: Joannes, of Hildesheim, d. 1375.
title: [The lyfe of the thre kynges of Coleyne]
text:
and is kept among great lords of that country/ And the print of these pence is on the one side a kings heed crowned. and on that other side it is written with letters of Chaldee. the which writing men can not red now/ And one of them is work ten shillings. or better than three florins/ And many more merueylies been told of these thirty pence. of whom it were a long process to tell/ ¶ Also when our lady and joseph were warned to come out of Egypt by an angel as the gospel telleth/ then they were bidden to go in to Galilee. and there they dwelled in a city which was called Nazareth/ And so the prophecy was fulfilled( Quoniam nazarenus vocabitur) that is to say He shall be called a man of Nazareth/ ¶ And what christ died work in earth from that time till the third year afore his passion. the Evangelists openly declare not in their gospels/

When our lord Ihesu Criste was stied up in to heaven. after that he sent saint Thomas th' apostle in to Ynde to preach there God's word/ In which Ynde as it is aforesaid these three kings the time reigned & were lords of those lands And though it so were that saint Thomas against his will go in to the lands of Ynde. yet it was done of great providence of god. that the same apostle the put his hand in to God's side to know the he was very god the was risen fo death to life for salvation of man should go & preach the Passion of Cryst. his resurrection. & his ascension to those worshipful kings that sought our lord in Bethlehem in his birth. and there with gifts worshipped him/ ¶ And as saint Gregory saith) Quod omnibus nobis ꝓfuit ꝙ hij tres reges eiusdem dni nostri ih̄u xpi infanciam que sierunt et oculis viderunt et devotissime muneribus adoraverunt & probaverunt) that is to say/ It was profit to us all that these worshipful kings & their people sought the childhede of christ. & with their eyen died see him. and with their gifts worshipfully & devoutly honoured him and soothly proved it/ ¶ Also the saint Barthylmew. Simon & Jude that were Cristis apostles were sent in to Ynde to preach the faith among all the people/ For there been many parties of Ynde/ And one part of Ynde is more than all the party of the world on this half of the see/ For this party of Cristendom on this half the see is no more accounted in all theest but an hundred days journey/

AFter that saint Thomas th' apostle had preached in the kingdom of Ynde God's word & had gone about all the Yndes & the provinces & done many miracles thorough the sign & token of the Cross & of God's word/ As he go about in the temples he found a star painted in every temple after the star that appeared to the three kings when christ was borne.

author: Joannes, of Hildesheim, d. 1375.
title: [The lyfe of the thre kynges of Coleyne]
text:
they bless the water and wash their cross in the water/ And seek men and blind men gone in to the water naked. and wash them. & after ward been heeled/ And when this is done every sect gone home again in to their owne-countree/ ¶ And between this jordan & Ihe/ rusalem is a little wilderness that is called Montost. and therein dwelled saint john Baptist. and there he preached/ And there our lord Ihesu Cryst came to saint john to be christened of him/ And in that same desert god almighty fasted xl days & xl nights/ ¶ Also bishops & other priests of what tongue or sect that they been. every day after their mass they say this gospel) Cum natus esset ihuns( as we in this country say( In principio) after our mass. But each sect saith in his own tongue & not in latin. safe on the twelve day only/ But it is read diversly right as it was done/ For in Iherusalem it is read thus) Aum natus esset john's in bethlehem in diebus herodis. hic regis ecce magi venerunt ab oriente hic dicentes( And in Bethlehem and in all the dyocecyse about it is read thus) Aun natus esset john's in diebus herodis hic & Jude regis & c̈( Also other christian men by whose places these three kings in their going out and coming home again passed by/ for a special devotion that they have to the three kings they red this gospel after this manner of four me( Cum natus esset john's in bethlehem iude in rebus herodis regis ecce magi regis gloriosi cum marima festinacione & excercitu ab oriente venerunt & per nos transierunt( And thus all divers sects read this gospel as it was done among them/ ¶ Also the saracens the believe on Machomites law & Turks have these three kings in special reverence in all temples of the country. they were sometime christened. & forsook it. & destroyed all the images in their temples. & cut of their noses & disfigured them for despite/ But the images of the three kings they suffer alway stand still without any despite/

furthermore touching the sects of Heretics aforesaid/ The first sect is called Nubiani. & those been of the kingdom of Araby & Nubie. whereof Melchior was king. & these been christian men/ And they have a special prerogative tofore all other christian men. for worship of their king/ And the priests of the country when they go to th altar have crowns of gold or overgylt on their heeds And the they do in tokening the the three kings with crowns on their heeds offered gifts to god almighty in Bethlehem/ & with crowns & miters sing their masses/

There is also another sect that is called Soldini. and they been of the kingdom of Godolie & Saba there Balthasar was king/ They were a party corrupt in the faith. & they took their names of an heretic that was called Solodinis/ But these men been not hold in so great reverence as the Nubiani.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
and they of the Isles call his the lady of the country / and shelyeth in and old castle and showeth his thryes in the year. And she doth no man no harm / & she is thus changed from a damsel to a dragon thorough a goddess that men call Deane / & men say that she shall dwell so unto the time that a knight come that is so har¦dy that dare go to his and kiss his mouth and than shall she turn again to his own kind and be a woman & after that she shall nat live long. And it is nat long sythen a knight of Roodes that was hardy and doughty said that he would kiss his & when the dragon began to lift up his heed again him and he saw it was so hydious he fled away▪ and the dragon in his anger bore the knight on a roche and of that roche she cast him into the see and so was he lost. Also a young man that wist nat of that dragon▪ went out of a ship and went thorough the isle till that he cam to a castle / & cam into the cave and went so long till he fond a cham¦ber / and than he saw a damsel that kempt his heed and looked in mirror and she had Much Treasure about his and h trowed she had been a common woman that dwelled there to keep men. and he obeyde unto the damsel. & the damsel saw the shadow of him in the mirror / & she turned toward him / and asked him what he would and he said he would be paramour or leman. And she asked him if he were a knight. and he said nay. And she said that might he nat be her leman. But she bad him go again to his fellows and make him knight and come again on the morrow. and should come out of the cave: and bad him come and kiss her than on the mouth / and she bade him have no dread for she should do him no harm if all him thought she were hydious to see. she said it was done by enchauntement. for she said that she was such as he saw his than and she said that if he kyst his he should have all that treso¦re and be his lord. And lord of those isles. and he depar¦ted from his and went to his fellows to ship and made him knight / and came again upon the morrow for to kiss the damsel. And when he saw his come out of the ca¦ue



in form of a dragon he had so gréaté dread that he fled too the ship / and she followed him / and when she saw that he turned nat again she began to cry as a thing that had Much sorrow  and she turned again and as soon the knight died.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
that he would help his that it might be known to all men. And when she had thus said she entered the fire and as soon was the fire out. and thoose branches that were brenning became red roses and those branches that were not kindled becam White rosers full of White roses and thoose were the First roses and rosers that any man saw and thus was the maiden saved thorough the grace of God. And therefore is the field called the felled of God flourished for it was full of rooses. Also beside the queer of that church at the right side as men come downward .xii. grees is the place. where our lord was born that is now full well dight of marble and full ry¦chely depeyntyd of gold silver and assure / and other colours. and a little them by three pacys is the Crybbe of the ox and the ass. And beside that is the place where the star fell that led the three kings Iasper Melchior and Balthazar. But men of Greece call the kings thus. Galgalath Saraphy Galgalagh. Theyse iii. kings



offered to our lord. Encense gold and myrrh & they cam together through miracle of God for they met together Ī a cite that men call Chasak. that is lui. iournes from Betheleem / and there they were at betheleem the fourth day after they had seen the star. And under the cloister of this church xviii grees at the right side of the Charnel of the Innocentis where their bones lie / and before that place where Christ was born is the tomb of Saint Ierom that Was a pressed and a cardinal that translated the bible and the sauter from Ebron to Latin. and beside it chur¦che is a church of Saint Nycholas where our lady rested his when she was delivered of child. And for as mo¦che as she had so Much milk in his paps that grieved his she milked it out upon the red stones or marble. so that yet may the traces be seen White upon the stones. & you shall understand that all that dwell in betheleem a Christian men and there are fair wines all about the cy¦te and great Plenty of wine for their books that macho meet betook Them. the which they call Alkaron. And sōme call it alkaron. and sōme call it Massap. and some call it harm forbedeth Them to drink wines: for Ī that book machomete curseth all those that drink of it wine & all that fell it for sōme men said ones that he slow a good hermit which he loved Much in his drunkenness And therefore he cursed the wine / and Them that drink Wyne. but his malison is turned to him self as holy writ Say. Et in verticem ipsius iniquitas eius descendet. That is to say in english: His wickedness shall descend in his own heed. And also the Sarasyns bryngethe forth no



grise ne they eat no swines flesh / for they say it is bro¦cher too man and that it was forboden in the old law.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
and Ierusalem is c. forlonges from this see / and so it is called the dead See. for it renneth nat. no man be'st that hath life that is therein may live and that hath been proved many times. for they cast therein men. that are deemed to death / ne no man may dwell▪ ne drink of that water / and men cast iron therein it cometh up again. And if a man cast a feather therein it Goth too the ground / and that is against kind. And there grows trees that bear fruit of fair colour and seem ripe. but when a man brekethe Them or cut in Them he findeth nought in Them but coals of ashes in tokenynge you thorough vegeaunce of God. These cities were brent with fire of hell. and sōme men call that lake. the lake of the alphitedde  and sōme call it the flome of the devil / and sōme the flome of stynkande. for the water is stinking There sank these five cities thorough wretch of God / That is to say / Sodom  Gomor  Aldema  Solo  me &


egor. For the sin of Sodom that reigned in Them but Segor through the prayer of Loath was saved a great while for it sat on a hill and yet appeareth Much thereof above the water / and men may see the walls in clear wedyr. And there Loath dwelled a great while and was made drunken of his Daughters and lay by Them. they trowed that God should have destroyed all the world as he did with Noah's flood. And therefore they lay by their fader. for men should be born of Them into the world. And if he had nat be drunken / he had nat lyen by them And at the right side of this see dwelled loath is wife a sto¦ne of salt for that she looked again when the cite sank down. ¶And you shall understand that Abraham had a son that he called Isaac / and he was circūcysed when he was of viii. days old. and therefore the Jews died circumcise Them at the age of .viii. days and he had another son than was called Ismael and he was of xiiii year of age when he was circumcised on a day. and ther¦fore the saracens did circumcise Them at xiiii. year old And into that deed see renneth the Flom Jordan and ma¦keth end there. And this Flom Jordan is no great river but there is Much Good Fish Them▪ and it cometh from mount Lybany. for two wells that men call Ior and Daue. and of Them it taketh the name. and upon the one side of that river is mount Gelboe. and there is a fair plyne. And on that other side men go by more Lybane to the Desert of Pharao / These Hills depae the kingdom of Surry and the country of Phenys. On that hill grow Cedres that berelonge apples Whych ar as Much as a mannys heed

¶This flom Iordane departeth Galyle: and the Land of Idones and the Land of Botron  and it renneth into a plain that men call Meldane in Sermoys and in that plain is the temple Iob.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
and theraboute is many good Hills and fair and many fair wodes and wild bestis And he that will go another way he Goth by the plains of Romayn costande the Roman see. On that cost is a fair castle that men call floraghe. And when a man is out of the Hills he passeth thorough the cite of Moryache and Artoyse where is a great Bridge upon the Ryuer. of fere that men call fassar. and it is a grea¦te river bearing ships  & beside that cite of Damas is



a river that comes from the mount of Lybany that men call alban at passing of this river Saint Eustache lost his two sōnes Whan he had lost his wyffe. and it goothe thorough the plain of arcades. and so to the red see. and so go men to the cite of Phenne and so to the cite of Ferne. And Antioch is a fair cite and well walled for it is two mile long. and at eke pylour of the Bridge is a Good tour. This is the best cite of the kingdom of sur¦y. Fro Antioch men shall go to the cite of Locuth / and than to Geeble. and than to Tortouse. And thereby is the Land of Cambre where is a strange castle it men call Manbek. And from Tourtouse men go to trypelle on the see. and upon the see men go to Dacres. and there is two ways to Ierusalem. on the lift way men go first unto Damas by flom Jordan. on the right side men go thorough the Land of Flagme / and so to the Cyte of Cayphas / of which Cayphas was lord / and sōme call it castle pellerinz / and from them it is four days Iourne to Ierusalem. and they go thorough Cesary Phylyp and Iaffe and Rames and Emaux. and so to Ierusalē

NOwe have▪ I told you sōme ways by Land / & by water. how men may go to Ierusalem. If all it be so that there be many other ways that men goo by after countries that they come from. Neuertheles they turn▪ all to one end▪ yet is there a weigh all by Land too Ierusalem and pass no see from France or Flanders but it weigh is full long & a {per}ylous & of great travail / & therefore few go it weigh. he that shall go that weigh he goes



thorough allemagne and Pruysse. and so unto Tartary This tartary is held of the great Cane of Whome I shall speak afterward / for theder lasteth his lordship And the lords of this Tartary yield him Trybute. this is a full evil Land and sondy and little fruit bearing. for there grows little Good of corn or wine ne benes ne pesen. but bests are there great Plenty / and therefore eat they but flesh Withoute breed / and they soup the bre and they drink milk of all manner of beasts.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
Iob was a paynim and also he was Coraas son / and he held the Londe as prince thereof / and he was so rich that he knew nat the hundredth of his Good. and after his pouert God made him richer than he was before. For after he was King of Idumea: and sithen king of ysan. and when he was King he was called Iohab and in that kingdom he lived Clxx year / and so he was of age when he died ccxl viii· in the Land of Iob is no default of no thing that is needful to a mannys body. There been Hills where men find māna. and māna is called angels bred that is a white thing right sweet and Much swetter than sugoure or honey. and that comes of the dew of heaven / that falls on the herbs / and there is coagles and wex White and men do it in medicines. for rich men. Thys Land marches to the Land of Caldee that is a great lon¦de. and there is full fair folk and well apeyraled and women a right layth and evil clad and they go bore foot / and bear a ill coat large wide and short unto the kne: & long slones down to the foot / & they have great here / and long hyngynge about their shoulders. After the land of Caldee is the Land of Amosony that is a lon¦de where is no man but all women as men say. for they will suffer no man live among Them ne to have lordspyp of Them. For sometime was a King in that Land and men were dwelling there as did in other coūtrees. and had wives / & it befell it the King had a great war with Them of Sychy and he was called Solopenco / &



he was slain in batyle and all the Good Blood of his Land. And this queen when she herd that / and other ladies of that Land that the King & the lords were slain they gathered Them together and slowghe all the men that were left in their Land among Them / and sithen that ty¦me dwelled no man among them. And when they will have and man to lie by Them they send for Them into a country hat is never to their Land / and the men come and ar there viii. days or as the woman likes and than goo they again. and if they have men children / they send Them to their adders when they can eat and goo. and if they have maid children they keep Them and if they be of gentle Blood they bren the left pap away for be¦rynge of a Shield. and if they be of little Blood they bren the right pap away for shotynge. For those women of that country ar Good wareours and ar oft in sonde with other lords and the queen of that Land governeth well that Land.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
And if you will weet how the Trees bear mele I shall say you. men hew▪ with and hachet a¦boute the  etre by the earth so that no berke be per / said in many places and than comes out a lycoure thy which they take in a vessel and put it to the son & dry it and when it is dry they do it unto the mill to grynde and so is it fair mele and White / and honey / and wine: and venom ar draw out of other trees in the same manner and do it in vessels to keep. In that Isle is a dead see / that is a water that hath no ground / and if any thing fall therein it shall never be found. beside that see grow¦eth great cans and under their rotes men find precy¦ous stones of great virtue. for he that beareth one of though stones upon him there may no iron dear him ne draw Blood on him. and therefore they it have these stones fight full hardly for there may no quarrel / ne such thing dear



Them: therefore they that know the manner of them they make their quarrels without iron and so they sle Them And than is another Isle that men call Calonach that is a great Land and a pleneuous of gods. And the King of it Land hath as many wives as he will. for he ha¦the a thousand and more and lieth never by one of them but ones. And that Land hath a marvel that is in no other Land. For all manner of fishes of the see cometh a time of the year every manner after other. and sayeth Them never the Land and on the Land sometime and there they lie three days. and men of the Land come theder & take of Them what they will. and than go those fishes away  and cometh another manner and lieth other three days and men take of Them. And thus does every ma¦ner of fishes till all have be there: and men have taken of eueryhone what they will. And me  nat the cause why it is. But they Say there. that  ishes continued / me so teder to do worship to their King. for as the most worthy King of he world for he hath so many wives. and geteth so many children of Them. ¶And than is a neither Isle that men call Gaffolo. Men of this Isle when there Friends ar seek that they trow it they shall die they take & hang him up all quick on a tre say it is bet¦ter y• birds it ar aūgellis of God eat Them than worms of the earth Fro them men go to and isle therethe men ar of ill kind they nourish hoūdes for to worow men & when their friends are syke it they hope they shall die / they do those hoūdes strangle thē for they will nat it they dykynd¦ly death for than should they suffer to great pain as they Say & when they ar thus dead they eat their flesh for venison



¶A from them men go through many Isles by see unto and Isle that men call Melke there is full ill folk for they have none other delight but for to fight and sle men for they drink gladly mannys Blood which Blood they call God.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
That is for to say Chane gods son Em{per}oure of all those that till all the Land and lord of all lords. and the writing above his gre¦ate seal is Deus in celo. Chan su{per} terram enis fortitudo oim hoīm im{per}atoris sigillum̄. That is to say thus God in heaven. chan upon earth his strength. The seal of the em{per}oure of all men / and the writing a bout his privy seal is thus. Dei fortitudo oīm hoīm im{per}atoris sigil / lū. That is to say the strength of God seal of the emperor of all men. And all if it be so that they be nat Christian: yet themperour & the tartaryns trow Ī God almighty

NOWe have I told you why he is called the gre¦ate chane. Nowe shall I tell you of the governing of his court when they make great feasts & the principal four times in the year. the First feste is of his bearing. the secoūd when he is born to the temple to be circūcised. the third is of his idols when they Begin to speak. & the forth when the idol beginneth First to do miracles & at those times he hath men well arrayed by thousādis & by hūdres & echone wot well what he shall do for there is first ordained iiii. thousand rich barons / and mighty for to ordain the fist and to serve the Emperor / and all these barons have crowns of gold well



dight with precious stones and pearls and they ar clad in clothes of gold and camathas as richly as they may be made  and they may well have such clothes for they ar there of less price than Woollen cloth is here. And these iiii. thousand barons ar departed in iiii. parties & eke company is clad in dyuers colour right richly. & when the first thousand is passed and hath showed them / than come the second thousand / and than the third / and than the forth and none of Them speaketh a word. And on oh side of the mperours table sitteth many philosophers of many sciences. some of astronomy nygromancy / geo¦metry / pyromacy / and other many sciences. and some ha¦ue before Them astrolabes of gold or of precious stones full of sonde or of cools brenning. some have orlages well dight and richly and other many instruments ter their sciences. & at a certain hour when they see time they Say to men that stand before them make psalm. & than say those mē with a loud voice to all the hall owe be syll a while. and than say one of the philosophers he man make reverence and bow and love to thempe¦roure that is gods son and lord of the world for now is time & hour. and than all men lout to him / & knee on the earth. and than biddeth the philosopher them rise up again. and at one other hour another philosopher bid Them all put their singers in their erys and they do so.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
but at one side & there is see of gaspy. And some men might ask. there is a see on one side / Why go they nat out there. for thereto answer I that all if it be called a see. It is no see / but a stange standing among Hills / and it is the gretteste stange of all the world. And if



they went over the see they wot nat where forto aryue. for they can no speech but their own. and you shall vnder¦stonde that the Jews have no law ef their own law in all the world. but they that dwell in these Hills / & yet they pay tribute for their Land to the queen of armony. And sometime it is so it some of the Jews go over the hyl¦les but many men may nat pass there samen for the hil¦les ar so great and so high. Neuertheles men say in that country there by that in the time of antecryst they shall do Much harm to Christian men. And therefore all the Jews that dwell in diverse parties of the world lere for to spe¦ke Ebrewe for they that the Jews that dwell among the Hills beforesayde shall come out of the Hills and they speak all ebrewe and nat else. and than shall these Jews speak ebrewe to them and lede Them into cristen¦dom for to destroy christen men. For these Jews say they Wote by their prophecies that those Jews that ar amon¦ge those Hills of Caspy shall come out & crysn men shall in their subiecion as they be under Christian men. & if you will wte how they shall find the passage out as I have understand I shall tell you. In time of and  a fox shall make his de in the same place where King alysaundre did make the gates and he shall so in there earth and pierce it through unto that he come amōg the Jews. And when they see this fox they shall have great marvel of him for they saw never such best. for other beses have they among them many. and they shall case this fox & pusue him unto that he be fled again into his hold that he cam from. and than shall they graven after as he went unto they come to the gates that



Alysaundre did make of great stones well dight with symont. and they shall break these gates and so shall they find the issue. From this Land men shall go unto the Land of Bakary where ar many wicked men and fell. In that Land ar trees that bear will as is it were sheep of which they make cloth. In this Land ar many Ipo¦taynes that dwell sometime on Land / sometime on water and ar half man and half Horse & they eat nat but mē when they may get Them. In this Land ar many gryf¦fons more than in another place.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text: and he chases and will sle the Olyfaunte. and there is many other manner of bests of whom it werē oh long to write. and there is another Isle Good & great and plenteuous where ar Good men and true and of Good life after their faith. and if all they be nat Christian. nevertheless of kind they ar full of Good virtues / and they sle all vices and all sin and malice for they are nat envious ne proud ne covetous ne lecherous ne glotenous / and they do nat unto another man but that they would he did do Them / and they fulfil the x. cōmaun / dementes / and they make no force of richesse / ne of having. and they swee nat but say nay / and you. for they say he that sweareth he will disceyue his neygboure. and some men call this the Isle of Bragamen and some call it the Land of faith and through it renneth a great river that men call Thebe. and generally all men in those I / ls and other thereby ar trewer and rightwyser than are in other countries. In this Isle are no thieves ne murde¦rers ne common women ne beggars. and for as Much they are so true and so Good that there is no tempest ne thunder ne war ne hunger ne other tribulations. and thus seemeth well that God loves Them well and is well pay¦de of their troth and their deeds and they trow in God that made all thing and him worship they and they lie / ne so ordynatly in meet and drink that they live right long and many of them die without sickness you kind faileth Them for age. And King alexander sometime sent his men to win that Land. and they sent him letters that said thus. What behooveth a man to have all the world may nt suffice thou shalt find no thing in us why thou shouldst warrey us for we have no riches. ne Treasure. and all the gods and cattle of our country ar common. our metes that we eat ar our richesse. And in stead of Treasure of gold and silver we make our tre¦soure peas and accord of love. and nought have we but a cloth upon our bodies. our wives are nat arrayed richly to pleasing. for we hold it a great folly a man to dyght his body to make it seem fairer than God made it. we have be evermore in peas till now that thou wilt disherit us. We have a king among us nat for to law ne deem no man. for there is no trespassoure among us but all only to lere us to be obedient to him and so may thou nought take from us but our Good peas. And when alexander saw this Letter. him thought thus that he should do to Much harm if he troubled Them. and sent to Them that they should keep well their Good manners / & have no dread of him.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: [Here endeth the boke of Iohn Maunduyle.
text:
and a little time after when he / & his counsel had examined it all thorough he said to me for certain that all was sooth. for he said he had a book of Latin it contained all that and Much more of the which the Mapa¦mundi is made the which book I saw. and therefore the holy fader the pope hath ratyfyed & confirmed my book in all points. And I prey to all those that rede this bo¦ke that they will prey for me / and I shall prey for them and all those that say for me a Pater noster and and Aue maria that God forgive me my sins. I make them {per}ceuers and grant Them part of all my Good pylgryma¦ges



and other Good deeds which I ever did or shall do to my lives end and I prey to God of whom all grace cometh that he will all the reders and hearers that ar christen̄ men fulfil of his grace / and save them body and soul and bring Them to his joy that ever shall last he that is in the trinity fader / son / and holy ghost that lyuethe and reigneth God without end amen

Emprented by Rychard Pynson. Richard pynson

author: Malory, Thomas, Sir, 15th cent.
title: [Le morte d'Arthur]
text: And then by assent of sir Trystram they wolde by assent of sir Trystram they wolde haue lodged together. But sir Dynadan wolde not lodge in that castle / & thenne he cursed the time that ever he came in their felaushyp / & so he took his horse & his harneys and departed / then sir Trystram prayed the lords of that castle to lene him a man to bring him to a lodging / & so they dyde & ouertoke sir Dynadan and road to their lodging two mile thence with a good man in a pryory & there they were well at ease. And that same night sir Bors & sir Bleoberys & sir Ector and sir Dryaunt abode still in the same place there as sir Trystram fought with the .xxx. knights / & there they met with sir lancelot the same night / and had made promise to lodge with sir Colgreuaunce the same night. but anon as the noble knight sir lancelot herde of the shield of cornwall then wist he well that hit was was sir Trystram that fought with his enemies / & thenne sir lancelot praised sir Trystram and called him the man of most worship in the world. So there was a knight in that pryory that height Pellynore / & he desired to wete the name of sir Trystram but in no wise he could not / & then sir Trystram departed & left sir Dynadan in the pryory / for he was so weary and so brysed that he might not ride. And then this knyʒt sir Pellynore said to sir Dynadan / sythen that ye will not tell me that knights name / then will I ride after him and make him to tell me

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
Tres vidit et unum̄ adoravit. That is to say / he saw three and worshipped but one / & him took Abraham in to his house. ANd right never to that place is a cave in a roche where Adam and Eve dwelled when they were driven out of Paradyse / and there gate they their children. And in that same place was Adam made as some men say / for men called some time that place the field of Damasse / for it was in the lordship of Damasse / and from them he was translated in to Paradyse as they say / And afterward he was driven out of Paradyse and put there again / for the same day that he was put in to Paradyse the same day he was dry uen out / for as soon he sinned. And there beginneth the vale of Ebron that lasteth never to Ierusalem / and the angel bad Adam that he should dwell with his wife / and there they engendered Seth of the which kindred Ihesu Christ was born. And in that vale is the field where men draw ou to of the earth a thing / the which thing men in that country call Chambyll / and they eat that thing instede of spice / and they bear it to sell / & men may not graven there so deep ne so wide but it is at the years end full again up to the sides through the grace of God / & two mile from Ebron is the graven of Loath it was Abrahams brodsr. THan a little from Ebron is the mount of Mambre of the which mount the vale to ke his name / and there is a free of oak that the saracens call dyrpe that is of Abrahams time / that men call the dry tree / and they say that it hath been from the beginning of the world and was sometime green and bore leues unto the time that our lord died & so died all the trees in the world or else they failed in their hertes▪or else they faded / and yet is there many of those in the world. And some prophecies say that a lord or pryn ce of the west side of the world shall win the Land of promyssyon / that is the holy Land with the help of Christian men / and he shall do sing a mass under the dry tree / and than the tree shall wax green and bear fruit and leues / and through



that miracle many saracens and Jews shall be turned to the Christian faith / and therefore they do great worship thereto and keep it right besely. And all if it be dry it beareth a great virtue / for certainly he that beareth a little thereof on him it healeth a sickness called the falling evil and hath also many other virtues / & therefore it is held right precious.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
precious stones / and a box of Iaspes green with four figures & . viij. names of our lord within / and .vij. candelstyckes of gold / & four censers of



gold / & and awter also of gold / and four lyons of gold / upon the which they had Cherubyn of gold. xij. span long / & a tabernade of gold / and also. xij. trumpets of silver / & a table of silver / and. vij. barley loves / & all other relyhes that were before the Natyuyte of Ihesu. Also upon this Roche slept Iacob when he saw angels go up and dnwne & said. ere locus iste sanctus est et ego ig norabā. That is to say. Forsoth this place is holy & I wist it not. And there the angel chaūged Jacob's name & called him Israell. And in that place saw Dauyd the angel that slow the people with a sword & put it all bloody in the shethe / And in this roche was Saint Symeon when he re ceyued our lord in to the Temple / & on this roche he set him when the Jews would have stonedr him / and the roche ryued in two & in that ryft he hid him / & a star came done & gate him light And on this roche sat our lady & learned her saw ter. And there forgave our lord the sins to the woman that was taken & foūde in aduoutry / and there was our lord Ihesu Christ cyrcūcysed / & there the angel denoūced to Zacharye the Natyuyte of Saint John baptist / & there offered First Melchysedech breed & wine and water to our lord in tokenynge of the sacrament that was to come. And there fell Dauyd praying to our lord for mercy for him & for his people when he saw the angel slee his people / and our lord anon herd his



prayer / & therefore would he make the Temple in that place. But our lord Ihesu Christ forbad high̄ by and angel / for he had done treason when he die de slee ryas a good knight for to have his wife. And therefore all that he hadr ordained for to make the Temple he betook it unto Salomon his soon / and he made it & he prayed our lord that all those that prayed in that place devoutly and with good Heart that he would here that prayer & graūte that they asked ryghtwysly / & our loosed graūte it / & therefore Salomons soon called it the Temple of coūseyll & help of God. Without the doors of that Temple is and awter where Jews were wont to offer doves & turtylles / and in y• Temple was Zacharye slain / and on the pynnacle the Jews set Saint Iames on the earth that First was bishop of Ierusalem / and a little from this Temple on the right side is a church covered with leed that is called the scole of Salomon.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
And after come men to Sybola where the Arke of God was kept under Hely the prophet. And there made the people of Israell their sacrifice unto our lord. Also there spam ke our lord First unto Samuell. And there ministered God the sacrament. Also there never at the lift side is Gabaon and Rama Benyamyn of the which holy writ speaketh. After that come men to Sychem that some men call Sycar / and this is in the province of Samarytanes / and some time was there a church but it was all cast down / and it is now a fair vale and that full plenteuous / and there is a good cite in that vale that men call Neople / and so froms them it is a days Journey unto Ierusalem / and there is the well where our lord spoke to the woman Samarytane / and Sychem is .x. mile from Ierusalem & it is called Neople / that is to say the new town. And there never is the Temple Joseph Ia cobs soon that governed Egypte. Fro them were his bones brought & laid in that Temple / and thither came Jews often in pilgrimage with gre to devotion. Also in that cite was Jacob's dough ter Dyana ravished for whom her brother's slew many me. and thereby is the cite of Garysym when re the Samarytanes make their sacrifice. ¶ On this hill would Abraham have sacrefyed his soon Ysaac / and there never is the vale of Dotayn & there is y• cistern where Io seph was cast in of his brethren before it they sold him / and it is two mile to Sychar / & from them men come to Sa marry it men call Sebasten / & y• is the chief cite of that coūtree / & in that cite was the sete of the .xij. kinds of Israell / but it is not so great as it was / & there was Saint John baptist buried between two prophets Helyzeus & Abdon / but he was beheaded in the castle of Makaryn beside the deed see & he was translated of his disciples & buried at Samary / but there died Iulius apostata take his bones & brent Them / for he was it time Emperor / but the finger with the which he showed our lord saying. Ecce agnus dei. That is to say Beholde the lombe of God / & that finger might


    ecla the virgin died bryn and Hely the prophets. And therefore  say▪ Peter. Bonū est nos hic esse. faciamus tria tabernaculam &c. That is to say. It is good to us to be here / make we three tabernacles. And our lord Ihe sum Christ bad Them that they should say it to no man unto the time it he was risen from death to life And upon the same hill shall four angels sown their trumpets & raise all men it are deed to life / & than shall they come in body & soul to the Iugement / but the Iugement shall be in the vale of Iosaphat on Eesterdaye at the same time as our lord rose from death to life.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
But me




but it is so warm there in that isle that men's bal looks hang down to their shanks for the great dyssoluynge of the body. And men of the country that know y• manner do bind Them up full strey to & anoint Them with ointments made therefore for to hold Them up or else they might not live▪ In this Land & many other men & wȳmen say Them all naked in Ryuers and waters from vndren of the day to it be passes none / & they lie all▪ in water but the face for the great hete that is there / and the Women be not ashamed for the men. In this isle are the ships without nails of iron or bond for roches of adamande that are in the see would draw ships to Them. ¶ Fro this isle men go by see to the isle of Cana where is great Plenty of corn & wine / and the king of this


le was sometime so mighty that he hlde  yenst king Alexander with great strength. Men of this isle have many manner of believe and faith and have also diverse laws / for some do worship the son / some the fire / some the trees / and some the serpents or any other thing that theyin First met in the Morning / and some do worship symulacres and idols / but between symulacres and idols is no difference / and that I to understand images made to lyknesse of wha thing a man will that is not kindly for some image hath and heed as and ox / and some have thr or four heeds / one of a man or and Horse or and ox or of any other be'st that no man hath seen. And you shall understand that they that worship symulacres they worship Them as for worthy me


that were sometime / as Hercules & other that died many meruayles in their times. For they say they wot well that they are not God of kind that ma de all thing / but that they are well with God for the meruayles that they do / & therefore they worship Them. And So say they of the son for it chaūgeth oftimes for it gyveth sometime great he  for to nourish all things on ethe / and for it is of so great profit they wot well it is not God but it is well with God & that God loves it more than any other thing / & for this cause they worship it. And also they say their reasons of other planets and of fire also for it is profitable & needful▪ And of idols they say that the ox is the holiest best it they may find here in earth & Most profitable than any other for he does Much good & none ylle / and they wot well that it may not be without special grace of God / & therefore they ma ke their God of and ox the one half / and the other half a man / for man is the fairest & the best creature of the world.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
And in and other isle are men also that have their faces all plot without eyes or mouth and without nose / but they have their eyes and their mouth behind on their shoulders. And in and other isle are foul




men that have the lyppe above the mouth to great that when they sleep in the son they cover all their face with the lyppe. And in and other isle are little men as dwarfs & have no mouth but a little roūde hold & through that hold they eat their meet with a pipe / and they have no tongue & they speak not but they blow & wysple and so make signs one to and other. And in and other isle are men with



hanging eeres unto their knees. And in and other isle are wild men with hanging eeres and have feet like and Horse & may run fast / and they take wild beasts & eat Them. And in and other isle are men that go on their hounds & feet like beasts / & are all rough & will leap upon a tree like cats or apes. And in and other isle are men that go ever upon their knees merueylously and have on every foot. viij. . And in and other isle is folk that




is both men & women & have members of both for to engender with / and when they will they use both on a time & the other and other time / & they get children when they use the member of man / & they bear children when they use the member of woman. Many other manner of folk is in this isles thereabout of whom it were to long to tell all. TO goo from this isle toward the eest many Iourneys a man shall find a kingdom it is called Mancy & this in India the more / & it is Most delectable & Plenty of goods of all the worl de. In this Land dwell Christian men & saracens / for it is a great Land / & therein is. ij. M. great cities & other many towns. In this Land no man goes on begging for theris no power man / & the men would we berdes thin of here as it were cats. In this Land are fair women & therefore some men call y• Land Albany for the White folk / & theris a cite that men call Latorym & is more than Parys / & in it Land are birds twyes greater than it be here. and there is good cheap of all manner of vitals / 





In this coūtree are White hens & they bear no feathers but wool as sheep do in our Land / & women of that coūtree y• are wedded bear crowns up on their heeds that they may be known by. In this coūtree they take a be'st y• is called  & they ken it to go in to waters or vyners / and as soon he bringeth out of the water great fishes / & thus take they Fish as long as they mill to  Them needeth.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
And five or six great lords riden about him so that none other men shall come never him but if the Emperor



call any. And in that same manner with charyotte & such oostes rideth the Empress by and other side / & the Emperors eldest soon on the same array / and they have so Much people that it is a great marvel for to see. THe Land of the great Chane is departed in. xij. provinces / & eke province hath more than two thousand cities & towns. Also when themperour tydeth through the coūtree / & he passes through cities & towns / eke man makes a fire before his house & casts therein ensence and other things it gyve good smell to themperour. And if any men of religion it are Christian dwell never as themperour comes they meet him with procession with a cross & holy water / & they sing Veni crea tor spiritus with a loud voice. And when he see Them come he cōmaundeth the lords y• ride never him to make way it the religious men may come to him / & when he see the cross he does of his hat that is made of precious stones & great pearls / & it hat is so rich that it is marvel to tell and than he inclined to the cross. And the prelate



of the religious men say orisons before him & gyveth him the benyson with the cross / & he encly¦neth to the benyson full devoutly / & than the same prelate gyveth him some fruit of the number of .ix. in a plate of gold as peers or apples or other fruit / & than the Emperor takes one thereof & the other he gyveth to his lords / for the manner is sum he there that no straūge man shall come before themperour but he gyve him some what after the old law that say. Non accedat in spectu me inanis. That is to say. No man come in to my sight idle. And than the Emperor biddeth These religious men it they shall go forth so that men of his oost defoul them not. And those religious men that dwell where the Empress or the Emperors soon comes do in the same manner. THis great Chane is the myghtyest lord of the world / for prester Iohan is not so gre¦te a lord as he / ne the Sultan of Babylon ne the Enperour of Persy. In his Land a man hath hon¦dred wives / & some .xl. some more some less / and they take of their kin to wives all save their sisters of their moders / but their sisters of their faders other wives they take also / & they take also well their stepmother if their fader be deed / &



men & women have all one manner of clothing so that they may not be known but it women that are wedded bear a token on their heeds / and they dwell not with their husbands / but he may lie by which that he will.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Here begynneth a lytell treatyse or booke named Johan Mau[n]deuyll knyght born in Englonde in the towne of saynt Albone
text:
And also beyond it flood toward the wilderness is a great plain all sondy & gravelly among Hills / and in it plain gro we trees that at the rising of the son eke day Begin to grow / & so grow they to midday & bear fruits but no man dare eat of it fruit / for it is a manner of iron / & after midday it turned again in to the earth / so it when to e son goeth down it is no thing seen / & so does it every day And there is in it wilderness many wild men with horns on their hedes & right hideous / and they



speak not but grunt as swine. And in that coūtree are many popyniayes that they call in their lan gage pystak & they speak through their own kind as apertly as a man / & those that speak well would we long tongues & large & on every foot five toos. there are some that have but three toos and though same speak nought or very little. THis Emperor preester Iohan when he goeth to battle he hath no banner born before him / but he hath born before high̄ three crosses of fine gold & those are great and large & well dyght with precious stones / & for to keep eke cross is ordained a thousand men of arms & more than and hundred thousand on foot in manner as men ke pe a standard in battle in other places & he hath men without number when he goes to any battle against any other lord. And when he hath no battle but rideth with privy company than doth he bear before him but a cross of tree not painted & without gold & precious stones & all plain in token it our lord Inu Christ suffered death on a cross of tree. And also he hath born before him a plate of gold full of earth in token that his lordship & nobley shall torn to nought & his flesh shall torn



to earth. And also he hath born before him and other vessel full of Iewellys & gold and precious stones in token of his nobley & his might. ANd he dwelled commonly at the cite of Su see & there is his principal palace that is so rich that marvel is to tell / & above the pryn cypall tour of the palace are two pomels of gol de all roūde / & eke one of those hath two carbūcles great & large it shine right clear on the night And the principal gates of this palace are of pre cyous stones that men call Sardyn / & the borders of the bars are of ivory / & the windows of the hall & chambers are of crystal. And tables that they eat of some are of Emeralds some are of mastyk some of gold & precious stones / and the pylers that bear the tables are of such stones also & the greces on which the Emperor goes to his see where he sitteth at meet one is of mastyk and other of crystal and other of Iaspy green and other of dyasper and other of sardyn and other of cormlyn a neither of sempton / and that he sets his foot up on is of crysolytes & all These greces are bordured with fine gold and well dyght with great pearls & other precious stones / and the sides of his siege are emeralds bordured with gold & with precyus



stones / the pylers in his Chamber are of fine gold with many carbuncles & other such stones that gyve great light on the night / and all if the carbuncles gyve great light nevertheless there bren neth eke night.

title: Here beginneth the lyf of the moste myscheuoust Robert the deuyll whiche was afterwarde called ye seruaunt of god.
text:
ROberte hath taken leave of the hermit & is gone toward Rome there for to do his pe¦naunce. And when he came in to the cite he began to leap & run about the streets making hȳselfe

 as though he had been a foal / & the children in the streets see Roberte run in this wise and they after him shoutynge and crying & casting with mire and derte and all such filth as they found in the streets and the Burgeyses of the cite say in their windows and laughed and mocked with Robert Than when Robert had thus played the foal in ro¦me a certain season he came on a time to you Emperors court & see that the gate died stand open & he ran Straight in to the hall / & there he Ietted up and down from the one end to the other sometime he went fast and sometime softly and than he hopped and ran and other while he stood even Still / but he stood not long in one place. The Em¦peroure sing Roberte thus playing the foal. He said to one of his servants / see yonder is a fair and a well favoured young man / me thȳketh he is out of his mind the which is great damage / for he is fair & a well made man / go & gyve high̄ meet. ¶ This Emperors seruaūt died as he was com¦maunded & called Robert to him & would have gy¦uen high̄ some meet / but Robert would neither eat nor drink / & while Robert sat thus at the table them¦perour saw one of his hoūdes which was bitten with and other dog / wherefore the Emperor cast him a bone and the dog caught the bone and be¦gan to gnaw there on & Robert seȳge it leapt from the table & took it from him / but the dog fought with Robert for the bone & held fast the one end & Robert you other end / but Robert see it would be no better / but set him down on the groūde & gnewe

 on the one end of the bone & the dog on you other themperoure and they that looked here on / laughed at robert and you dog. but Robert died so Much it he gat the bone alone & say and gnewe it for he was soar enhongred. themperoure sing that Robert was so soar enhongred he cast to and other dog¦ge and hoole lofe. but robert took it From him & bra¦ke it in two pieces & gave the dog half for by cause he gat it for the dogs sake. thēperour sing this lough there at & said to his seruaūtes. We have here now the most foolish foal and the verayst needy that ever I saw for he takes the dogs meet from thē & eateth it himself thereby a mā may perfectly know that he is a natural foal all that were in the hall gave the dogs as Much meet as they might eat to tenteth it robert might fill his belie with thē & when he had filled his belly while he rose up and walked up and down in the hall with a staff in his hand / smiting upon stoles and ben¦ches like as & if he had be a very Innocent foal.

title: Here beginneth the lyf of the moste myscheuoust Robert the deuyll whiche was afterwarde called ye seruaunt of god.
text:
& incōtinent when this proclamation was done among the comyns every man was Willing & ready to go with themperour to fight & defēde their right and so they went forth in a fair ordinaūce with themperoure to fight upon their mortal enemies the heathen dogs / And for all you themperour had Much more people than the senshal yet the seneschal had won the field / had not God of his great marry sent theder Robert to resist and help the Romans in their extreme necessity. THe Emperor & the Romans went to the battle as said is against the saracens. & ro¦berte was at home. Where he was accustomed to walk in the garden to a fountain or well to drin¦ke. & this was on the same day that the emperor with his host should gyve battle against the sara¦syns. than there came a voice out of heaven sent fro¦me our lord above saying in this manner. Roberte God cōmaūdeth you by me that you incōtynent arm you with this harness and Light upon this horse that God hath sent you. & ride in all haste possible and rescue the emperor & his people. Robert herȳ¦ge the cōmaundement of God was abashed in his mind. and durst not do against gods commaūde

 but in cōtynent he armed him & leapt on that Horse without any tarrying and road his way / the Emperors daughter which I told you of before stood at a window & saw Roberte thus armed on Horse back than if she could have spoken she would have told it but she could not speak for she was dumb but she remembered and bore it surely in her mȳde Robert thus horst & harnayst road in to them¦perours Host which he saw was soar overpressed with their enemies the Turks in so Much it had not God & Robert rescued thē you Christian men had been all slain / but whā Robert was come in to thoost he put high̄ in you Most press of you turks & fought & laid on eke side on these cursed hoūdes / there a man might have seen / arms / legs / heeds tumble on the groūde / he smote to the groūde both Horse & man it never rose after / it was a world to see the murder it Robert died among the dampened dogs the sa¦rasyns / so to make short tale Robert died so Much it the saracens were cūstrayned to fly away & thē¦perour held the field & had the victory of them. NOw hath the Empererour goten you field & the honour thanked be God & Robert is turned again to the said fountain & there unarmed him & laid the harnays on the Horse which incon¦tynent was vanished away it no man could kno¦we nor perceive where he become and Roberte bode

 Still standing by you fountain / emperors dough¦ter sing this had great meruayll of this & would have told it forth but she was dumb & could not speak / Robert had a raze in his face which he goat in you battle / but he was none otherwise hurt / the Emperor was glad & thanked God of his victory against you false dogs you saracens & thus being me¦ry he came home to his palace & when they were all set to dinner Robert presented hȳselfe before thempe¦rour as he was wont to do plaȳge you foal & makyn¦ge high̄ dōbe as a before rehearsed is themperour rejoiced in hȳselfe when he see Robert for he loved high̄ passyn¦ge well & than̄ he perceived roberts hurt in his face & thought it some of his seruaūtes had hurt him while he was out / wherefore he was angry & said / here in this court be some envious men / for while we have been out at battle they have beten & hurt this poor Innocente creature in his face which is great sin for though he be a foal he does no man harm so thēperour cōmaūded them all upon a gre¦te pain it no man should do high̄ harm / if they died they should be punished it all other should beware by them / than themperour began to axe his knygh¦tes if there were any of thē it could tell of you knight with the White Horse it came privily in to the field & so valyaūtly rescued thē thēperours daughter this hearing pointed themperour her fader it it was ro¦berte / but themperour understood not what his dou¦ghter mente what she poȳted / for she could not spe¦ke / wherefore he called her masters to him & axed her what his daughter mente by her pointing / &

 her mistress answered and said your daughter menes by her pointynge that this day you have got¦ten the battle and victory thorough the help of your foal robert & the raze that is in his face he ha¦the got it in the battle.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Than is there an other yle ye men call Dodye
text:
or .iiij. thousand / & he gueth them to eat of fair

vessels of silver / & when they have eaten he smiteth

the bell again & they goo again their way. And

the monk say y• those bests are souls of men it

are deed / & those beasts it are fair are souls of

lords & other rich men / & those y• are foul bests

are souls of other comunes. And I asked Them if

it had not be better to gyve that relief to poor men

& they said theris no poor man in you country & if

there were yet it were more alms to gyve it to those

souls you suffer there their penaūce & may go no

ferder to get their meet than to men you have wit

& may travail for their meet. Than come men to

a cite you is called Chybens & there was y• First siege

of y• kine of Mancy. In this cite are .lx. bridges

of stone as fair a they may be. WHan men pass from you cite of Chybens they

pass over a great river of Fresh water / &

it is never iiij. mile broad / & than men en¦tre

in too the Land of the great Chane. This Ryuer

goeth through the Land of Pygmeens / & there

men are of little stature for they are but three span



long & they are right fair both men & women

though they be little / and they are wedded when

they are half a year old / & they live but .viij. year

& he that liveth .viij. year is held right old / and

These small men are the best work men in silk &

of cotton in all manner thing that are in the world. & These small men trauaylne till no Land / but

they have among them great men as we are to tra¦uayle

for them / and they have great scorn of those

great men as we would have of giants or of

Them if they were among us. ERo this Land men go through many coun¦trees

& cities and towns till they come to

a cite that men call menke. In that cite is a gre¦te

navy of ships & they are as swyte as snow

of kind of the wood that they are made of / & they

are made as it were great houses with halls & cham¦bres

& other esymentes. ANd from them men go upon a river that

men call Ceremosan / & this river goeth

through Cathay & does many times harm when

it waxes great. Caythay is a fair coūtree & rich



full of goods & marchaūdyses / thither come merchants

every year for too fetch spices and other

machaundyses more comunely than they do in to

other coūtrees. And you shall understand that mar¦chauntes

that come from Venyce or from Geene or

from other places of Lombardy or of Romayne / 

they go byse and Land .xi.

author: Mandeville, John, Sir.
title: Than is there an other yle ye men call Dodye
text:
ANd you shall weet why he is called the great

Chane / you wot well that all the world

was destroyed with Noah's flood but Noe & his wife

& his children. Noe had three Sons Sen Cham and

Iapheth. Cham was he it saw his faders balockes

naked when he slept & scorned it / and therefore

was he cursed / and Iapheth covered it again. Thyse three brother had all the Land. Cham took

the best part eestwarde y• is called Asia. Sem

took Affryke / & Iapheth to Europe. Cham was

the myghtyest & richest of his brother / & of him

are come the paynem folk & dyuers manner of men

of the isles / some hedles / & other men dysfygured / 

& for this Cham the Emperor there called him

Cham & lord of all. But you shall understand that

the Emperor of Cathay is called Chane & not

Cham / and for this cause it is not long gone it all

Tartary was in subgeccyon & thrall to other Nations

about / & they were made herdemen to keep

beasts / & among Them was .vij. lineages or kinds / 

the First was called Tartary you is the best / the
